Household electricity and gas prices in the EU fell in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Prices rose in many European capitals in October, and households could face higher bills in early 2027.

Even as the Iran war started driving up wholesale gas prices, household electricity and gas prices fell on average across the EU in the first half of 2026.

The differences between countries were striking. A unit of electricity cost more than three times as much in Ireland as in Hungary, according to Eurostat.

Where in Europe did households pay the most and least for electricity and gas? And how do the rankings change when local price levels are taken into account?

Among 38 European countries with data, household electricity prices including taxes ranged from €6.6 per 100 kWh in Turkey to €38.7 in Ireland in the first half of 2026. Hungary had the lowest price in the EU at €11.4, while the EU average was €28.3.

In euro terms, Ireland was followed by Germany (€36.2), Belgium (€35.8), Austria (€32.6), Italy (€31.4) and Sweden (€30.6), all above €30 per 100 kWh.

Electricity prices were lower than the EU average in Spain (€25.1) and France (€24.9).

Romania has the highest electricity prices in purchasing power terms

Prices were generally lower in EU candidate countries, and the gap with the most expensive countries was large. That gap narrowed once differences in local price levels were taken into account using purchasing power standards (PPS).

Electricity prices ranged from 12.6 PPS per 100 kWh in Iceland to 46.9 in Romania. Poland (41.1) and Czechia (34.3) rounded out the top three, followed by Ireland and Italy at 32.8 each.

After Iceland, Turkey (13.5), Malta (13.8), Hungary (14.7) and Norway (15.0) had the lowest prices in purchasing power terms.

Among the EU’s four largest economies, Italy had the highest price (32.8), closely followed by Germany (32.4). Spain (28.0) was close to the EU average (28.4), while France (23.3) was cheaper.

Electricity prices rose sharply in Romania

Household electricity prices fell by 2.2% on average in the EU compared with the second half of 2025. Measured in euros, Finland recorded the largest rise at 19.5%, followed by Turkey (11.2%), Poland (10.6%), Lithuania (10.6%) and Sweden (10.4%).

Denmark (-28.2%) and Luxembourg (-24.1%) recorded the biggest falls. Prices in Italy rose by 5.9%, while they fell by 6.5% in Germany, 6% in Spain and 3% in France.

Compared with the first half of 2025, the EU average electricity price fell by 1.6%. Romania recorded the biggest increase in euro terms at 51.9%, followed by Turkey (35%), Ireland (19.8%) and Finland (18.4%).

Prices fell in all four of the EU’s largest economies: France (-7%), Germany (-5.7%), Italy (-4.5%) and Spain (-3.9%).

Government policies help explain why price changes vary, according to Professor Xiaoyi Mu, director of the Centre for Energy, Petroleum and Mineral Law and Policy at the University of Dundee. Taxes, levies and network charges make up a large part of final prices. Denmark, for example, temporarily cut its electricity tax by roughly €0.10 per kWh from 1 January 2026. Finland had no such tax relief.

Energy market intelligence firm VaasaETT, which helps compile the Household Energy Price Index (HEPI), has also pointed to differences in the energy mix, tariff structures, how suppliers buy and price energy, and how costs are shared between groups of customers.

Sweden has the most expensive gas

Across the 29 European countries with data, household natural gas prices, including taxes, ranged from €1.6 per 100 kWh in Georgia to €22 in Sweden in the first half of 2026. Hungary (€3.3) had the lowest price in the EU, where the average was €11.

The Netherlands (€16.2), France (€13.5), Portugal (€12.6) and Austria (€12.4) rounded out the top five.

Gas prices were above the EU average in France, Germany (€11.6) and Italy (€11.4), and below it in Spain (€7.9).

In PPS terms, prices ranged from 4.3 per 100 kWh in Hungary to 20.8 in North Macedonia. North Macedonia was below the EU average in euro terms (€10.8) and moved to the top of the ranking once local price levels were taken into account.

Sweden (17.7), Portugal (15.0) and the Netherlands (13.8) also ranked among the most expensive. At the lower end, Turkey (5.0), Luxembourg (6.6) and Croatia (6.8) had the lowest prices after Hungary.

Household gas prices fell by 10.2% on average in the EU compared with the second half of 2025. In euro terms, Italy (-23.2%), Spain (-17.6%) and Greece (-16%) recorded the largest falls. Turkey had the biggest rise at 12.9%, followed by Romania (6.3%).

Compared with the first half of 2025, the EU average fell by 3.5%. France was the only one of the EU’s four largest economies where gas prices rose year on year, up 3.7%.

Why do wholesale price rises take time to reach households?

The figures cover only about four months after the US and Israel began striking Iran in late February. The full impact on household bills may take longer to show up.

“There is always a lag between the benchmark wholesale natural gas price (TTF) and the prices paid by households,” Xiaoyi Mu told Euronews Business.

“The lag can range from a few months to more than a year, depending on how the retail energy market is organised in each country.”

Many households are on fixed-price contracts, Mu said. Suppliers cannot pass on higher wholesale costs while those rates are fixed.

Suppliers also often buy gas and electricity in advance to protect themselves against price swings. That can delay the impact of wholesale price changes on household tariffs.

Higher bills could come in 2027

Mu said Europe’s benchmark wholesale gas price fell by 19% in the second half of 2025 compared with the first half of that year, and by 14% compared with the second half of 2024.

“I believe this is one of the key reasons behind the fall in household energy prices in the first half of 2026 despite the subsequent increase in wholesale gas prices following the conflict in the Middle East,” he said.

“For this reason, unfortunately, I do expect households could face higher energy bills in the second half of 2026, but more so in the first half of 2027,” he added.

Across EU capitals tracked by HEPI, household gas prices rose by 12% on average between 2 February and 1 September, while electricity prices rose by 4.2%.

HEPI’s October update recorded electricity price rises in 21 of the 33 European capitals it tracks, and gas price rises in 14 of the 27 capitals with gas data.

Regular trips to the park from birth to age 11 are linked to better mental health and social skills in children, a new study has found.

Going to the park can help children’s mental health and social skills as they grow up, according to a new study.

Researchers found that children who were taken to the park at least once a week from birth to the age of 11 scored, on average, 16.5% higher in their mental health assessments than those who visited less than once a week over the same period. The benefits remained even after adjusting for socioeconomic status and family problems.

“Parks give children space to be physically active, which is known to support mental and physical health, as well as helping adventurous and imaginative play to build confidence and independence,” said lead researcher Mark Ferguson of the University of Exeter in the United Kingdom.

“We believe parks could be more than places to play, but an important resource for children’s healthy development,” he added.

The study, published in the journal Epidemiology and Community Health, included 4,219 participants and focused on social-emotional development — the skills children need to manage their feelings, build relationships, behave appropriately and cope with everyday challenges.

Strong social-emotional development is an important foundation for good mental health in childhood and later life, the authors noted.

The study found that children tended to show better social-emotional development during periods when they went to parks more often. Children who visited parks more frequently overall also fared better than those who went less often.

Park visits were associated with improvements in both internalising behaviours, such as emotional symptoms and peer problems and externalising behaviours like conduct problems and hyperactivity or inattention.

Researchers also examined whether park visits and social-emotional development varied according to family background. Children from more advantaged areas appeared to visit parks more frequently at a younger age, while those from less advantaged families tended to visit more often as they grew older.

The study suggests parks and playgrounds could help reduce inequalities in children’s development, but only if they are easy for all families to use.

For parks to be beneficial, “communities need good-quality parks that are safe, accessible and welcoming to families from all backgrounds,” said Ferguson.

Because parks are free and open to everyone, they can have an “equigenic effect.” This describes how certain physical or social environments, most notably green spaces, can act as a levelling force that narrows health, psychological, or educational disparities between socioeconomic groups.

Scientists are mapping one of the world’s last wild ecosystems to help us ‘understand what we have lost elsewhere’.

Nesting turtles, fish-filled coral reefs, and mysterious deep-sea creatures: this is what scientists found in one of the world’s last largely untouched ecosystems.

Two remote coral atolls in the Pacific Ocean are being studied to support local and global conservation efforts.

Bikar and Bokak became the Marshall Islands’ first national marine sanctuaries in 2025. Since then, scientists have been working to establish a comprehensive ecological baseline for the 48,000-square-kilometre site, from sky to land and sea.

Their findings matter far beyond the remote atolls, which lie around 116 and 385 kilometres from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.

“They are among the best ecological reference systems we have to better understand what we have lost elsewhere and to provide fundamental insights needed for effective conservation and restoration efforts,” says marine ecologist Dr Alan Friedlander of the University of Hawai’i.

He served as chief scientist aboard a joint expedition in Bikar and Bokak with Pristine Seas, a global conservation and exploration project founded by National Geographic Explorer Enric Sala to help protect vital ocean areas.

What they found were “some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region” – and perhaps the world.

‘Treasures for the entire planet’: What the world can learn from remote ecosystems

Extensive monitoring of Bikar and Bokak in 2023 informed the creation of the protected area.

Researchers were guided by the Marshall Islands’ national framework for community-led conservation, which seeks to protect natural resources “while ensuring island life thrives for generations to come”, explains Friedlander, who led a recent study on the atolls’ ecosystems.

“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” he says.

While the atolls have recently gained national protection, they have long been cared for through community-led stewardship, with high chiefs establishing ‘mo’ or ‘taboo’ areas. In these zones, human activity is restricted, allowing nature to rest and replenish – an approach that has been incorporated into the national framework.

It has resulted in an ecosystem that offers an unparalleled glimpse into how life functions with only minimal human influence.

“The Marshall Island government should be applauded for their foresight in protecting these global biodiversity hotspots, where human activity is distant and habitats teem with life,” says Friedlander. “As human activities increasingly threaten biodiversity, areas devoid of intense human impacts serve as vital refugia.”

Large marine protected areas like these are globally important benchmarks for understanding how tropical ocean ecosystems are structured and how they may change in an era shaped by human activity, the researchers say.

Remote atolls teem with life while wildlife is in decline elsewhere

Bikar and Bokak offer a rare contrast to most of the world. Monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73 per cent globally since 1970, according to WWF’s 2026 Living Planet Report, with marine populations down 59 per cent.

Bleaching-level heat stress hit 84 per cent of the world’s coral reefs between January 2023 and May 2025, and only around 3.5 per cent of the ocean is considered fully or highly protected.

Using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea cameras, and a submarine, Pristine Seas scientists explored Pacific ecosystems that, by contrast, remain relatively intact.

Across both atolls, they found 15 breeding or likely breeding seabird species and more than 260 kinds of reef fish, as well as open-water predators including sharks, jacks and wahoo. Cameras and a submarine also revealed “surprisingly diverse and poorly known deep-sea communities”, and two of the fish recorded might be new to science, the researchers say.

Nesting green sea turtles were also observed at Bikar.

Ecological differences between the two reefs were noted, although the researchers say the reasons are not yet clear. Bokak’s reefs are dominated by coral, with around twice the fish biomass of Bikar, where seaweed covers more than half of some deeper slopes.

The project also highlights the importance of assessing ecosystems in their entirety in order to conserve their integrity and track future climate-driven change, the researchers say, adding that future studies should examine nutrient transfer and ecological connectivity between habitats.

Even with responsible local governance, the most isolated tropical reef systems aren’t immune to the global impacts of human-caused climate change. They are increasingly affected by coral bleaching, ocean warming, sea-level rise, and changes in how much food the open ocean produces, the study warns.

The Happy Passports Index ranks 50 countries on everything from life satisfaction and civil liberties to passport strength and income, and the results are surprising.

A powerful passport might make it easier to see the world, but does it actually make you happier? A new ranking of 50 countries suggests the two don't always go hand in hand – but, often, they do.

The research behind the ranking, published by Global Citizen Solutions, a migration firm offering second residency and citizenship solutions, looked at 50 countries and how happy their residents are, how free they are at home, how far their passports travel and how well they live.

These cover everything from how people rate their lives and the civil liberties they enjoy to passport access, income, life expectancy and peace. The idea is to measure not just how easily people can travel, but how happy and free they are where they live.

All those factors added up to a score out of 100 in the Happy Passports Index ranking – and here’s what it shows.

Nordic nations come out on top

The Nordic nations are famous for the happiness of their residents, so it’s little surprise that they all come near the very top of the ranking.

Finland leads with 93.2 out of 100, and is closely followed by Iceland, with a score of 92.4 and Denmark, which was awarded 92.1.

Norway is in fourth, and Sweden comes in sixth place, with scores of 89.3 and 88.2, respectively.

Switzerland, another very wealthy nation with happy residents who boast strong passports, was in fifth, with a score of 88.3

Wealth and strong passports don’t necessarily mean a high placement in the ranking, though.

For instance, Singapore has the highest income and the longest healthy life expectancy as well as the strongest passport in the sample, but it only comes in at 10th place, held back by its wellbeing (23rd) and freedom at home (30th) scores.

The UK has a strong passport, which gives holders wide travel access, but it ranks 29th of 50 both on people’s sense of freedom to make life choices and on civil liberties. That equals a placement of just 17th in the overall ranking.

“The happiest countries tend to hold strong passports, but not always,” said Dr Laura Madrid, Lead Researcher at Global Citizen Solutions. “Among wealthier countries, our briefing finds that happiness correlates far more strongly with freedom than with passport strength. That is because a passport offers something different: choice beyond the border.”

More mobile, but not necessarily happier

Among wealthier countries, the index found that freedom to make personal choices was much more closely linked to life satisfaction than either passport strength or income.

Malta, Portugal, Japan, Cyprus, Malaysia, Spain and Greece all score well for passport access and healthy life expectancy, but their residents report lower levels of happiness.

All seven rank higher overall than they do for life satisfaction alone.

Portugal is a particularly striking example, coming 21st in the overall index despite ranking 39th for how people rate their lives.

The index’s findings suggest, then, that being able to travel widely doesn't automatically make life better at home.

Why balance matters more than wealth

New Zealand, Australia and Malta all make the top half of the rankings across most measures, despite falling outside the top ten for both wealth and passport strength. New Zealand, for example, ranks just 25th for income but eighth overall.

The common factor is a fairly even performance across the different measures, rather than excelling in just one.

That’s particularly clear for Costa Rica, Uruguay, Mexico, Panama, Brazil, Israel and Saudi Arabia, which all score highly for life satisfaction despite having less powerful passports, underlining that travel freedom is only one part of the picture.

One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, recounted that he was at work when his wife phoned and said that their two children, aged 2 and 7, were among those trapped in the rubble, local media reported.

At least two people have died, while others have been trapped in the rubble after a three-storey building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York, at the edge of a construction site on Wednesday afternoon.

Some 250 firefighters and police officers tackled the rubble with pickaxes and saws to pull people covered in dust from beneath piles of twisted wood and brick.

During a press conference, officials said that at least 17 people had been hospitalised, four in critical condition. While it is unclear whether people might still be trapped, New York City Fire Department officials stated that search and rescue operations would continue into the night.

“This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for.”

According to New York City’s Buildings Commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, the building fell when construction workers were digging an empty lot next door for a new building. However, the cause of the collapse is under investigation.

The collapsed building, which housed apartments above ground-level businesses, was reduced to a massive mound of debris at the bottom of the construction pit. The neighbouring structure, which shared a wall with the building, was left standing but suffered extensive damage. Much of its exterior wall had been ripped away, leaving the interiors exposed, including a bedroom and closets with clothes still hanging inside.

One of the survivors was a woman who was pulled from the rubble by firefighters late in the afternoon after a hole had been dug through the debris. Meanwhile, more people continued to be pulled from the rubble as search and rescue operations proceeded, including seven children, although officials did not specify whether any of them were among the dead.

FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the rescue teams, who were digging by hand and using drones to carry out operations, were performing “dangerous and perilous” work. “Every move is choreographed,” she said.

One firefighter was left with minor injuries, according to fire officials.

One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, recounted that he was at work when his wife phoned and said that their two children, aged 2 and 7, were among those trapped in the rubble, the New York Post reported.

“She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off,” he said.

Velez said he later found out that his family had been rescued from the rubble alive.
